#3258. Apple’s funny new Apple Card ad features an awkward therapy session

Apple shared a new Apple Card ad on its YouTube page today featuring a therapist who realizes she really needs a vacation. Watch it below.

In a new ad shared today, Apple showcases how easy it is to apply for an Apple Card and start using it right away.

The ad shows a therapist who gets distracted mid-session by a notification about a flash sale on flights to Jamaica on her iPhone, but realizes her wallet is too far away to act on it.

As her patient continues talking about his problems, she quickly applies for an Apple Card through the Wallet app and uses it to book the flight, all without him noticing, but just barely.

#3257. Google takes over the Wyoming data centre site Crusoe had planned

The AI data centre developer is handing over the site a day after Google pledged $17B there.

Google has bought Crusoe’s data centre site in southeast Wyoming and will build the project itself, after pledging $17B there. Bloomberg had reported Crusoe was pushed aside after failing to sign customers. Terms were not disclosed.

Google has bought Crusoe’s data centre site in southeast Wyoming and will build the project itself, Crusoe said on Friday. Neither company disclosed the terms.

The deal comes a day after Google said it would spend $17B on its first Wyoming data centre, in Laramie County. It ends Crusoe’s early work on the site, which included choosing the location, winning government approvals and planning its power supply.

Crusoe announced the project with Blackstone-backed Tallgrass Energy in July 2025, saying it could eventually grow to 10 GW. In June, Crusoe was being pushed aside after failing to sign customers, with Google raising concerns about costs and timing, Bloomberg reported.

Crusoe said it still has more than 6 GW of capacity under contract and over 40 GW in its pipeline. It is also building a data centre campus for Google near Amarillo, Texas, and raised $3.9B at a $30.9B valuation in September. Elsewhere it has landed customers, including deals with Meta in June and a reported $13B contract with Jane Street.

Developers face a tougher climate. Several new governors elected this week have promised to rein in data centres, Bloomberg said, and voters rejected data centres in 40 of 41 local ballot measures.

#3256. watchOS 27.3 adds new Apple Watch feature that I absolutely love

watchOS 27.3 arrived this week in beta alongside iOS 27.3, with a major new feature for the latest Apple Watch models: Siri Recap, which I’m already really loving.

If you bought an Apple Watch Series 12 or Apple Watch Ultra 4 this fall, there are two exclusive new features coming in watchOS 27.3: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Both ‘Audio Intelligence’ features were announced at Apple’s September keynote, but just debuted in beta this week.

Siri Recap in particular has stirred some controversy. Here’s what the feature does, per Apple:

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Siri Recaps can be set to automatically delete after a period of up to 7 days unless you choose to explicitly save them.

It’s understandable why users would be concerned. Once enabled, Siri Recap can turn your Apple Watch into a device that’s always listening and often takes notes on what it hears.

Speaking strictly of the functionality of Siri Recap itself, however, I’ve been very impressed.

I enabled Siri Recap after installing the iOS and watchOS 27.3 betas on Tuesday. When I checked the first recaps on Wednesday inside the Siri app, I was blown away.

Siri had created a record of the things I’d done Tuesday afternoon and evening with remarkable accuracy and detail, as seen above.

One example that especially shocked me: after shopping for Christmas decorations with my family, Siri documented the size of a table runner we looked at. The thing is, I had no memory of anyone even mentioning its size. My wife must have, but despite me missing it, Siri wrote it down.

Another fun one: Thursday morning during breakfast, my son wanted to listen some music on our HomePod. Later that day, I found that the songs we’d listened to were saved at the bottom of my latest recap.

It’s still very early days with Siri Recap, which is only in beta right now, but what I’ve seen this week has been really exciting. And so far at least, I’ve seen zero information in a recap that I’d consider too sensitive to be included.

What’s your take on Siri Recap? Have you given it a try? Let us know in the comments.

#3255. Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream

Nearly 70 percent of respondents say they want an AI assistant in their next device, according to a new report

Qualcomm builds intelligent, connected, computing and AI solutions that transform industries and advance human progress.

A recent report by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide, shows that around 70 percent of respondents express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.

This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies.

For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules?

It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user.

These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want?

A Personal AI report, commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments.

The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI.

Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor.

Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction.

With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report.

The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit.

The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users:

But for all the excitement and engagement around intelligent wearables, there’s a gating factor: trust. As use cases for intelligent wearables expands to more personal and persistent experiences, trust is a necessity for Personal AI.

Notably, the report found that respondents expressed more interest in adopting intelligent wearables when Snapdragon was introduced as the enabling platform. This reinforces the value of having an established, trusted technology foundation in the mix.

The report shows that consumer appetite for AI is high, with 60-70 percent of those surveyed expressing interest in advanced AI as they consider a new device. That’s a constant. But remaining purchase drivers differed between device categories.

Audio playback quality is the most influential purchase driver for true wireless earbuds and headphones. For smartwatches, it’s display quality and responsiveness. Respondents are less concerned about technical specifications than aesthetics like materials and finish when it comes to devices like smart rings and pendants. And for smart glasses, it’s all about the type of control, whether it’s voice, gesture, or touch.

Artificial intelligence is entering a new phase, one that is deeply personal, continuously present, and seamlessly embedded into the devices we wear every day. This evolution, which we define as “Personal AI”, represents a shift away from generic, cloud-only intelligence toward AI that understands individuals in context: their habits, preferences, environments, and intent, in real time.

Alongside these purchase drivers is another key finding: Consumer appetite for Personal AI agents has gone mainstream. The report says that 70 percent of respondents “express strong interest in an AI assistant that can interact naturally through voice and seamlessly manage devices, apps, and everyday tasks.” With each individual as the center of their own ecosystem, voice becomes the most critical, natural method for interacting with agents.

Intelligent wearables comprise much of the hardware of this “ecosystem of you.” Consumers are interested in ecosystems instead of single devices, and they’re looking for agentic AI capabilities that understand and act on their behalf.

Yet so much of the industry remains undefined. OEMs and technology makers have an enormous opportunity right now to innovate and iterate on the strong technological foundations that platform makers are building. And the roadmap for what consumers want is clear.

All percentages, consumer behaviors, and attitudes stated in this report are based only on the responses of the individuals who participated in our survey.

Qualcomm Technologies is a global leader in communications and computing technologies, including leading-edge AI, high-performance, low-power computing, and connectivity solutions. Headquartered in San Diego, Calif., the company develops technologies for next-generation mobile networks and smart devices, and designs semiconductors such as mobile processors and AI chips.

The bias is deafening. Qualcomm, a chip manufacturer that is all in on AI, makes a survey and then states they found everyone loves using AI, the very AI that will run on Qualcomm chips. Clearly they don't have a conflict of interest in this. /s

#3254. AI teddy for three-year-olds gave unprompted self-harm reply, BBC finds

The BBC could not find who makes the £75 plush toy, which is sold online in the UK.

An AI plush toy marketed for children as young as three gave a self-harm crisis reply to a question that had nothing to do with self-harm, a BBC investigation found. The BBC published its findings on Thursday.

The toy, called Doubao, is sold online in the UK as My Baby Bunny for £75. A BBC Wales reporter asked it a series of questions about how babies are made. When she asked it to define the word sexual, it appeared to mishear her.

“I’m really sorry you’re feeling this way. I can’t help with killing you,” the toy replied, according to the BBC.

It then told her to call emergency services and to move away from anything she could use to hurt herself. When she said she had not mentioned self-harm, it apologised.

The BBC could not find out who makes Doubao. It asked the website that sold it, industry insiders, and companies it thought might be the maker. As a result, it could not ask anyone to explain the reply.

The BBC also tested Grem, a $99 toy from US firm Curio. Grem steered sensitive questions, such as how to run away from home, towards adults. Curio told the BBC that child safety guides its product development.

Paul Clarke, founder of Southampton-based AI toy maker Play Tech AI, said the result did not surprise him.

“We’re crying out for the industry to be regulated,” Clarke told the BBC.

Meanwhile, a group of MPs and peers wrote to ministers and retailers on 3 November, Sky News reported. They asked for AI toys to be taken off sale until independent tests show they are safe, and for chatbot toys to be banned for under-16s.

The UK government told the BBC that children’s safety is its top priority. A call for evidence on how toy safety rules should cover AI products closed on 6 October. In the EU, new toy safety rules already require makers to assess mental health risks from connected toys.

#3253. Report: Apple faces congressional scrutiny over ICE tracking apps and Trump donations

Reuters and The Washington Post report that Apple is among the tech giants potentially facing congressional investigations as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers in January. Here are the details.

Earlier today, The Washington Post reported that “Democrats are laying the groundwork to investigate some of the country’s largest companies, setting off a scramble among executives who courted the president.”

The report notes that Washington law firms are advising companies and executives on how to prepare for potential congressional investigations, with some also pitching their services to Elon Musk:

Multiple firms have crafted pitches for why they should serve as Musk’s personal counsel, aware that the world’s richest man is likely to receive a barrage of subpoenas and that any casework stemming from those investigations will be both lucrative and the highest-profile investigative work available in the coming year, according to two of the people.

When it comes to Apple, the report noted that lawmakers are gearing up to investigate the company “over its hosting of tracking apps used by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.”

While the report refers to Apple’s hosting of tracking apps used by ICE, the company has previously faced scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers over its decision to remove apps used to track ICE agents from the App Store.

Last year, Apple removed ICEBlock and several similar apps from the App Store following pressure from the DOJ, citing concerns over the safety of federal agents.

The move came shortly after a gunman opened fire on an ICE facility in Dallas, ultimately killing two detainees in an attack that federal authorities described as targeted violence against ICE.

Since then, Apple has faced questions from Democratic lawmakers over the extent of the Trump administration’s involvement in the decision and whether the removals infringed on constitutionally protected speech.

 or no , oversight needs to happen. If  did bad, let it come out; if not, let that come out as well. There should be no sacred cows here, oversight and accountability need to be our national, collective goal.

Reuters, meanwhile, reported that Senator Richard Blumenthal, “who is set to take over as chair of the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations,” called on Apple “and others who donated to [President Trump’s new White House] ballroom project to turn over records” or “face possible subpoenas in January.”

As The Washington Post reported last month, Apple and Nvidia each pledged $25 million toward the ballroom, making them two of the project’s largest donors.

Apple did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters or The Washington Post.

#3252. Multiphysics Modeling for Next-Generation Electromagnetic Manufacturing Technologies



Advances in sensing, manufacturing, computational resources, and data-driven methods are enabling new approaches to electromagnetic sensing, non-destructive evaluation, and advanced materials processing. This webinar will demonstrate how the COMSOL Multiphysics software supports predictive modeling by coupling electromagnetic fields with thermal, chemical, mechanical, and transport phenomena across multiple length and time scales.

The first application we will show focuses on eddy-current thermometry for reconstructing three-dimensional temperature fields in metal plates. Temperature-dependent electrical conductivity alters induced currents and magnetic fields, enabling volumetric thermal inference. COMSOL simulations of defects and laser-induced transient heating will support validation of reconstruction algorithms. Multifrequency excitation will be investigated to improve depth discrimination through frequency-dependent penetration depths and sensitivities.

The second application examines microwave-enabled volumetric additive manufacturing of ceramic components. A high-power microwave beamforming array delivers localized energy into three-dimensional volumes, enabling processing of opaque, particle-laden resins. Coupled COMSOL models of electromagnetic propagation, microwave absorption, heat transfer, and ceramic sintering kinetics are used to predict temperature evolution, reaction progression, spatial resolution, and processing scalability. Future extensions will incorporate pulsed excitation, fluid flow, resin viscosity, convection, shrinkage, and solid mechanics.

Together, these examples demonstrate how the COMSOL software can integrate multiphysics modeling with sensing, manufacturing, and data inversion. This webinar will present two applications of coupled electromagnetic and thermal modeling in COMSOL Multiphysics: eddy-current thermometry in metal plates and microwave-assisted processing of ceramic-loaded resins. By connecting simulation with practical engineering systems, COMSOL-based modeling can accelerate technology development, reduce experimental iteration, and support reliable scale-up of next-generation electromagnetic technologies.

From the historic Lambeau Field to the multi-billion-dollar spectacle of SoFi Stadium, we rank the very best NFL venues every football fan needs to experience

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Enjoying an NFL stadium encompasses so much more than the action on the field. When you watch a game with 70,000 (give or take) other folks, there’s a communal aspect to the event, one that includes tradition, technology and, of course, plenty of food. And not every NFL stadium experience warrants equal billing. Some traditions just run deeper, events feel richer, food tastes better and memories last longer.

Scouring stadiums is part of my gig. From donning a hard hat and climbing into the petals that make up the Mercedes-Benz Stadium retractable roof to exploring the bowels of Lumen Field or wandering the tailgating lots of Arrowhead Stadium to exploring every inch of SoFi Stadium, I’ve toured dozens of stadiums. Sometimes I’m with architects as they explain how sketches turned to steel, or next to chefs as they craft the latest concourse-ready concoction (salivating as I prepare to sample the creation, of course) or ensuring I don’t get grass stains as turf managers explain the intricate care required to keep the field in pristine shape. So I explored NFL stadiums for you, selecting seven spots worth the trip to gain a full picture of all that the NFL has to offer.

Tim Newcomb has covered the world of sports and stadiums across the globe, from Olympics to Super Bowls and FIFA World Cups to Final Fours, all four major tennis tournaments, the World Series, the NHL Finals and more.

Key Stats: Opened in 1972, Arrowhead Stadium hosts 76,000 fans. Known for its ocean of parking lots around the stadium—more than 19,000 parking spaces—the Truman Sports Complex turns into a tailgating mecca.

The Vibe: Clad in the red of the Chiefs, the Arrowhead Stadium fan knows their football and comes for a day of celebration that includes food, chants and raucous exuberance (a powerful 142.2-decibel crowd roar in the stadium’s history punctuates this) that just may feature two-time NFL MVP and three-time Super Bowl MVP Patrick Mahomes running the offense.

Tailgating: If you’re going to tailgate in one NFL Stadium across America, this is where to do it. Set up shop in your own parking spot or enter the Chiefs’ Tailgate District for food trucks, entertainment and experiences, all four hours before the game starts. Tailgating is a way of life, with recipes passed down through generations and fans setting up in the same stall for years.

Technology: You don’t go to Arrowhead for the glitz and glamor of technology (part of why the Chiefs actually plan to move away from the stadium), so take in a bit more of an old-school charm, although the venue features an HDR display Arrowvision board in the east end zone, while hundreds of Sony 4K displays pepper the venue. A continuous LED ribbon board encircles the seating bowl. Arrowhead features high-density Wi-Fi, 5G DAS, walk-through security, mobile ticketing and, for the players, an underground field heating system.

The Food: Obviously K.C. features barbecue. And plenty of it. Find your favorite, whether the popular Joe’s Kansas City Bar-B-Que or the Smoak BBQ for the brand-new pork belly bomb with cream, Boursin, parmesan, sour cream-and-onion chips, candied thick-cut bacon and red pepper jelly.

Insider Moves: Register with the team as a designated driver and receive a free water or soda.

The Must-Experience Moment: Have we mentioned the tailgating? Taking in the Chiefs Hall of Fame is a must-see attraction for fans but exploring tailgating before kickoff reigns king.

The Bottom Line: Experience the Midwest hospitality in a sea of red by eating your way through the day, from well before the game to during it while experiencing a classic football experience inside the Arrowhead Stadium bowl.

Key Stats: Opened in 1957, Lambeau Field and its 81,000 seats is the second oldest stadium in the NFL.

The Vibe: No other NFL venue says community like Lambeau. Tucked into the fabric of Green Bay and its neighborhoods, the team is as much a part of the local way of life as any professional sports team in the country as the only publicly owned professional team.

Tailgating: Yes, please do and try it out in the stadium parking lots, neighborhood lawns, church parking lots and nearly anywhere you can wedge a vehicle and a grill into the same spot.

Technology: You’re not here for the tech, but you’ll find it at the field level where the stadium became the first in the United States (in 2007) to use a hybrid natural grass and artificial turf concoction. There’s also an underfield heating system (installed in 1967 and updated since), the first in the NFL. While still highly traditional, Lambeau Field features ultra-high-definition LED boards in both end zones with integrated stats and replays and a wrap-around LED ribbon board. Fans can stay connected with high-density Wi-Fi and 5G DAS and enjoy digital ticketing, walk-through security and grab-and-go self-checkout.

The Food: Maybe its cliché, but its cliché for a reason: Get the Johnsonville brat with the Sargento fried cheese curds. They’re a must and quintessential Green Bay. If you want to step it up, the “horse collar” makes a 10th anniversary return, a Johnsonville kielbasa sausage topped with beer cheese sauce, beer mustard and sauerkraut on a horseshoe Kaiser bun.

Insider Moves: First timers can find a stadium worker and get a first-game pin or button. Also, keep in mind most of the seats are traditional aluminum benches, so you can bring in your own cushion or rent a cushion and seatback for $10.

The Must-Experience Moment: Take in the neighborhood feel on the way into the stadium but also stop at Titletown on the way for live entertainment and activities. The must-stop moment comes inside the main stadium and the Packers Hall of Fame to view the team’s Lombardi Trophies. Of course, make sure to watch for a Lambeau Leap when a Packer scores a touchdown.

The Bottom Line: Buy a cheesehead and embrace the historic nature of Lambeau Field, taking in the community feel and history of the stadium and surrounding site while watching a game with a passionate fan base.

Key Stats: Opened in 2017 for 71,000 fans, a 16-story-tall window looks out from the stadium to downtown Atlanta.

The Vibe: Decidedly more urban and modern than the first two classics on the list, Mercedes-Benz Stadium also has a more social feel and not the intensity you may get from some NFL venues.

Tailgating: Atlanta features tailgating lots but also tailgating on grassy lawns in The Home Depot Backyard, a distinct differentiator for the venue.

Technology: Take in the Halo Board inside the venue. At 58 feet tall and ringing the entire seating bowl, the 63,000 square feet of technology was a first of its kind in sports and rewrote the way teams presented the fan experience. Plus, the steel petals that form the roof make one of the most intriguing retractable roof designs in stadium history (although the roof typically remains closed for games). There’s also a 101-foot-tall “Mega Column” LED wrap and over 2,000 LED displays across the venue. The more than 4,000 miles of fiber optics include under-seat Wi-Fi and 5G with walk-through security and Just Walk Out tech on the concourse.

The Food: You can afford it! The leader in fan-friendly pricing, a hot dog is only $2, nachos $3, pizza $4 and a cheeseburger $5, to name a few. The $20 Board features chicken strips, fries, nachos, a hot dog, a slice of pizza, a soft pretzel, popcorn and a drink in one box. Of course, you can go bigger with some specialties, such as a Big Dave’s Cheesesteak with grilled ribeye (still only $11 without the onions and $12 with).

Insider Moves: It’s all about the fan-friendly food, where the soda purchase gets you a free refill throughout the game.

The Must-Experience Moment: Take in the falcon statue outside gate two on your way in and then make sure you participate in the call-back “Rise Up” chant as you’ll be prompted to throughout the game.

The Bottom Line: An urban, modern experience, Mercedes-Benz Stadium takes some of the best of what a stadium experience should be and mixes in social and technological aspects to create a fresh stadium feel.

Key Stats: Opened in 2002, the stadium seats 68,000 fans, including about 70% of them under a 760-foot-long metal roof that helps reverberate crowd noise back to the field.

The Vibe: The Seahawks get loud with their 12th Man moniker, fighting with Arrowhead Stadium for the title of loudest stadium in the NFL (in 2011 nearby University of Washington recorded seismic activity from the stadium during a playoff touchdown and their loudest decibel reading is 137.6).

Tailgating: Sadly, no, the dense urban location of Lumen Field eliminates tailgating from Seattle, so fans instead flock to nearby restaurants and bars or experience some of the street food on Occidental Avenue surrounding the venue.

Technology: Known for its ability to handle the crush of phone use, connectivity is typically impressive at Lumen Field as there’s enterprise-grade high-density Wi-Fi and 5G DAS. The stadium features numerous locations of Amazon’s Just Walk Out technology and there’s even checkout-free pro shop outlets and Amazon One biometric scanners at stores and concessions. Both end zones feature Mitsubishi Electric diamond Vision HDR boards and express walk-through security.

The Food: Grab a Seattle Dog (they add cream cheese and grilled onions in the Emerald City) along Occidental Avenue on your way in or get one inside the stadium. This season try out the special menu created with wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba with jerk salmon nachos and jicama steak noodles.

Insider Moves: With no tailgating, Lumen Field allows fans to bring their own single-serve food items into the venue if in a clear bag.

The Must-Experience Moment: Hike to the top of the Hawk’s Nest for a unique look at Lumen Field and then turn around to see downtown Seattle (with views of Mount Rainier a bonus on a clear day). Oh, don’t miss the raising of the 12th Man Flag during pregame.

The Bottom Line: A distinctly Pacific Northwest experience with an extra dose of noise, Lumen Field ensures a sea of blue fans will yell their way through a game with much of the focus on the in-bowl experience.

Key Stats: Opened in 2016 for 66,000 fans, the fully enclosed stadium features a 240,000-square-foot ETFE transparent roof, the largest in the United States.

The Vibe: You best like purple, as Vikings fans fill U.S. Bank Stadium with a loud passion that proliferates purple throughout.

Tailgating: With a downtown stadium, tailgating has a limited footprint in Minneapolis, but the Vikings Village creates a fan festival atmosphere with food, entertainment and activations.

Technology: That ETFE transparent roof comes fritted to deflect heat and UV while letting natural light into the venue. LED video displays pop up in both end zones while a continuous LED ribbon board covers both the lower and upper seating bowl and hundreds of additional HD monitors fill the site. High-density enterprise Wi-Fi and 5G DAS help with connectivity, and the stadium features walk-through security.

The Food: The signature Skol Dog features bacon jam and purple potato chips, but there’s also those gooey cheese curds at Curds & Cakes. Another popular option is the raid burger, a double-bacon cheeseburger with buffalo cheese curds and an onion ring. Of course, there’s a chuleta kan kan pork chop available with pickled veggies, guacamole and tostones.

Insider Moves: Instead of going to the west gate like most fans, gain entry quicker at the north or south gates.

The Must-Experience Moment: Don’t miss the Skol Chant, always done before the start of the game and often revisited in the second half.

The Bottom Line: Experience a passionate fan base in the comfort of an indoor venue that still has a feel of being outside with the transparent roof. There’s plenty to do in and around the stadium to keep you entertained beyond the football on the field.

Key Stats: It’s brand-new, opened in 2026 for 61,000 fans and with a cantilevered canopy that covers approximately 65% of all fans.

The Vibe: The hard-nosed culture of Buffalo Bills football comes to life in the outdoor venue. Even in the brand-new Highmark Stadium, the region embraces the elements and celebrates the industrious feel of western New York.

Tailgating: Like much of Buffalo, tailgating comes with a layer of extra. The tailgating culture permeates the vibe of Buffalo and the table smashing—there’s even a smashed table highlighted inside the stadium—is now a staple of the experience and one of the top tailgating sites in the country, all led by the Bills Mafia. It’s no different with the move across the street.

Technology: The best technology comes in the form of fan comfort, with the new stadium now featuring infrared heating sent to most fans in the bowl, a first-of-its-kind snowmelt system on the roof and an underfield heating system. There’s Cisco Wi-Fi 7 and its 1,300 access points, along with hyper-directional DAS help with modern connectivity. And fans enjoy AiFi Tech’s cashier-free markets and walk-through security.

The Food: You’ve gotta get wings when in Buffalo, right? Check out the Highmark wings and Mumbo wings in the stadium but don’t look past the poutine and pierogies or the blue & red burger with Treasure Cave blue cheese, red onion and bacon jam. If you want another taste of Buafflo, go for the beef on weck with a Wegmans kimmelweck roll, top round, au jus, horseradish and dill pickle.

Insider Moves: If you own a Toyota, show your keys at the Toyota Fast Pass at gate two for quick entry.

The Must-Experience Moment: You must swing through the tailgate experience before the game, taking in the culture of Buffalo at every step. With a new venue, make sure you visit the “family circle” of bison outside the stadium and then head up to level three for views out to the surrounding area.

The Bottom Line: This is Buffalo, but with a bit more comfort. The new Highmark Stadium looked to preserve the feel of outdoor football in the elements for the players, but brought in some fan-friendly comforts—a canopy and heating, for example—for the fans while accentuating the Buffalo traditions of tailgating.

Key Stats: Opened in 2020 for 70,000 fans, the most expensive stadium ever built ($5.5 billion) sits 100 feet below ground due to its proximity to LAX and features 20 million holes in the aluminum panels that make up the stadium’s skin.

The Vibe: It’s a spectacle of immense proportions, from the expansive site to the architecture to the technology. SoFi Stadium is a venue unlike any other; while just doesn’t have the diehard football feel of some of the classic venues on the list (or not on this list, mind you, with apologies to Baltimore and Pittsburgh) that means it trends more corporate, befitting its status as a multi-time Super Bowl host.

Tailgating: It’s not a culture that permeates the venue, but it’s still available on site, although a fan zone filled with food trucks is more the feel at SoFi.

Technology: Yes. Plenty. The world’s first dual-sided video board, dubbed Oculus, is 120 yards long, 70,000 square feet in size and offers 4k resolution, remaking what’s possible with in-venue video. It’s a site unlike any other in sports. There’s also continuous LED ribbon boards wrapping multiple levels of the seating bowl, thousands of Sony 4K/IPTV displays in the concourses, In addition, there’s Wi-Fi 6 from Cisco with 2,500 access points (some under seats or in handrails), 5G DAS, walk-through security and plenty of touch-screen ordering kiosks and grab-and-go concessions.

The Food: We’ve got burritos aplenty, from chopped brisket to shrimp, but check out the Chile relleno burrito and the fish tacos. Of course, you can always go for the pastrami frites or the twinkie burger featuring a beef patty, American cheese and a Texas twinkie (a brisket-stuffed jalapeno).

Insider Moves: If your seat is high up, wander down to standing-room-only spaces to catch a new view of the game, hit the American Airlines Plaza button bar on level six for a free custom button and think about using the Uber Eats app to skip concession lines and pick up your food at a dedicated spot.

The Must-Experience Moment: Really, to take in all of what SoFi Stadium has to offer, wander the entire site both outside the venue and once inside, grasping the uniqueness of the architecture and the experience that goes beyond the football.

The Bottom Line: SoFi Stadium is about more than football. It’s about the experience across the grounds. For a completely different football gameday, check out SoFi Stadium.

His favorite interviews have included sit-downs with Roger Federer in Switzerland and Kobe Bryant in Los Angeles.

#3250. When Electric Cars Were for Women

Early carmakers decided women wanted cars that were quiet, clean, and easy to start

Allison Marsh is a professor at the University of South Carolina and the codirector of the Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society.

When automobiles were still a novelty, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion.

At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.

Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with.

Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.

In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

A young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it.

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty Images

Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.

The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery.

I couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.

This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & Gardens

According to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.

Bailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.

While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).

Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & Gardens

Goodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.

When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.

Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and Science

Although Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.)

Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.

Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.

Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.

An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

References For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)

For a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.

Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Allison Marsh is a professor in Women and Gender Studies at the University of South Carolina and codirector of the university’s Ann Johnson Institute for Science, Technology & Society. She combines her interests in engineering, history, and museum objects to write the Past Forward column, which tells the story of technology through historical artifacts. Marsh is currently working on a book on the history of women in electrical engineering.

#3249. House chairs ask Nvidia’s Jensen Huang to explain reported spy link

They want a closed-door briefing on 18 November about his contacts with a former Megaspeed executive.

NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang during his GTC 2026 keynote at the SAP Center in San Jose, 16 March 2026

The request follows a New York Times report on 29 October. The Times said US spy agencies had watched Alice Huang for about a year over her ties to China. Officials feared she could learn about Nvidia’s plans.

The Times also reported that officials did not believe Jensen Huang knew she might be gathering information for China. Neither of them has been charged. The two are not related.

Megaspeed, a Singapore firm that buys Nvidia chips, has said it hired outside lawyers to look into the claims, Forbes reported. US officials have also looked into whether the company helped China get restricted Nvidia chips.

It is not clear whether Huang will attend. Nvidia did not say when asked by Semafor on Friday.

“We’re confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo told Semafor.

Huang has said no to Congress before. In June, he declined Senator Elizabeth Warren’s invitation to testify on Nvidia’s sales to China. Warren is expected to chair the Senate Banking Committee next year, Semafor reported.

#3248. iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more

This week, Apple released the first iOS 27.3 beta. The update includes multiple new features for iPhone users, including the redesigned Health app, iPhone Duo updates, and much more. Here’s everything you need to know about what’s new in iOS 27.3 …

As my colleague Ryan explained, Apple will likely release iOS 27.3 to all iPhone users sometime in December. Typically, Apple would release its x.2 software updates in December, but this year is different because iOS 27.1 was exclusive to iPhone Duo. That means that, in terms of the timeline, iOS 27.3 is essentially the equivalent of iOS 27.2.

Here’s when Apple has released its December updates in recent years:

So with that in mind, we expect iOS 27.3 to be released sometime during the first half of December.

The redesigned Health app is back in iOS 27.3. This was first available during testing of iOS 27.2, but did not ship as part of that final update.

The redesigned Health app is split into three tabs: Insights, Longevity, and Browse. The app features an all-new design that dynamically adapts based on your data, including Apple Intelligence. The Longevity tab includes a new Health age feature that uses Apple Watch data to show how your metrics track relative to your actual age.

For Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 users, it also offers easy access to view your Readiness score every morning.

For Apple Fitness+, iOS 27.3 adds a new Gym Strength feature. This creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment.

As you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weights you logged.

For iPhone Duo users, iOS 27.3 adds Reachability support. This setting shifts the interface on the outer display to the right or left to make it easier to reach the far corners. It’s designed to make iPhone Duo easier to use with one hand, despite the wider outer display. You activate it by swiping right on the right edge of the screen or left on the left edge.

Reachability for iPhone Duo is on by default. You can turn it off in Settings > Accessibility > Touch > Reachability.

iOS 27.3 also tweaks the iPhone Duo’s software keyboard by making the keys slightly narrower and the font slightly smaller.

When it debuted, the iPhone Duo included a more robust version of StandBy with new clock faces and expanded customization options. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s StandBy experience to all iPhone models.

This includes the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces, as well as additional customization options for colors and complications. The update also adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face.

iOS 27.3 brings several key Siri AI updates. First, the update expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps. Apple explains:

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference. To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

With iOS 27.3, Apple is also starting to test new ways for developers to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. This is described as an “early Developer Preview.” Apple explains:

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more. So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

While this is being tested as part of iOS 27.3, Apple says it will start shipping to customers in a few months.

iOS 27.3 also expands Siri AI to new languages, including French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

iOS 27.3 brings the original set of Apple Intelligence features to China for the first time. This does not include Siri AI or other iOS 27 updates, but it does include the following features:

iOS 27.3 is a major update to Safari. First, the update adds support for a new vertical tabs design layout on iPhone Duo’s inner display. If you choose this option, your Safari tabs will be arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari, rather than along the top. Vertical tabs are also available on Mac and iPad with macOS 27.3 and iPadOS 27.3.

iOS 27.3 also adds a new Adaptive Dark Mode feature. This feature can automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t natively support it. You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

For Apple Music users, iOS 27.3 adds a new “Selfie Sing” feature that lets users record a video of themselves while singing karaoke. To use this feature, start playing a song and go to the lyrics view. Then tap the new camera button that appears on the right-hand side of the lyrics.

The update also refines the design of viewing lyrics while your iPhone is in landscape mode.

Read more: – iOS 27.3 upgrades Apple Music in two ways, here’s what’s new

Here are a few other changes in iOS 27.3:

What are your favorite new features in iOS 27.3? Have you spotted any other changes in the update? Let us know down in the comments.

This intense thriller expands its twisted world

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Based on Stephen King’s 2019 novel of the same name, “The Institute” is a sci-fi thriller series that first premiered on MGM+ in July 2025. Starring Ben Barnes, Mary-Louise Parker and Joe Freeman, the adaptation quickly made an impression with audiences, recording one of the best premieres in the streamer’s history.

Now, the King adaptation is back, with the story continuing beyond the events of the original novel. As a fan of the first season and this genre in general, I have plenty of thoughts.

Season 2 picks up following Luke Ellis (Joe Freeman) and his friends’ escape from Dennison, as they set out to bring the Institute down for good. However, their freedom doesn’t mean they’re out of danger, with the organization already working to rebuild under the direction of a powerful new ally, tech billionaire Nolan Reeves (Alfie Allen). Meanwhile, Ms. Sigsby (Mary-Louise Parker) finds herself on the outside looking in and is determined to find a way back into the organization. With more secrets to uncover and new threats emerging, the fight against the Institute is far from over.

I’ve watched the episodes ahead of their official release on MGM+ and I’m ready to share my honest thoughts on whether this Stephen King adaptation is worth your time. From its expanded storyline and returning characters to the new additions and twists, there’s plenty to get stuck into now that the first episode is streaming.

I’m Alix, a lifelong horror nerd who loves watching, reviewing and writing about the latest movies and TV shows. When I’m not working through my ever-growing horror watchlist, I’m covering the biggest releases across streaming and film, including the latest DC movie "Clayface," "VisionQuest" on Disney+, and "Crystal Lake" on Peacock.

Season 2 picks up almost immediately after the events of the first, with Luke and the others having escaped the Institute and desperately trying to put as much distance between themselves and the organization as possible. We initially find them fleeing on the back of a train before jumping forward four months, where the group is now hiding out in a disused construction site.

Tim (Ben Barnes) is still recovering from his bullet wound, but the experience has left him tougher and more guarded, particularly when it comes to keeping the children safe. Meanwhile, Luke’s precognition abilities are kicking into full swing, making him more determined than ever to track down a specific flash drive that could bring the organization down for good.

The series takes a little while to find its feet, but things start to pick up as the episodes progress. That slower approach does at least give the characters more room to breathe, with the story regularly switching between Luke and the other children and the powerful figures pulling the strings behind the Institute.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

One of the most interesting additions is Nolan Reeves (Alfie Allen), an eccentric European tech billionaire who financially backs the organization. He’s not quite as straightforward as he first appears, and his own ambitions add another layer of mystery to the season. It’s nice to see the show introduce someone who could potentially be just as dangerous as the people already running the operation.

Joe Freeman and Ben Barnes remain two of the season’s biggest strengths, delivering performances that capture very different sides of the fight against the Institute. Freeman brings plenty of determination to Luke’s search for justice, while Barnes does a good job showing how Tim’s experiences have changed him and how much he fears losing the people he’s trying to protect. Not everything works quite as well, however. The developing love triangle between Luke, Kalisha (Simone Miller) and Nicky (Fionn Laird) is one of the weaker additions, particularly because their strongest connections have always felt rooted in friendship. It comes across as a little forced and doesn’t feel especially necessary.

Unfortunately, season 2 has lost some of the initial spark that made its predecessor so compelling. The first season had such an intriguing central mystery and a claustrophobic atmosphere that made the Institute feel genuinely unsettling, and that’s something the follow-up doesn’t quite manage to recapture. There are still some tense episodes and interesting developments, but the story occasionally feels like it’s revisiting familiar ground, with certain plot points and structural choices feeling a little too similar to what we’ve already seen. Still, there’s enough here to keep fans invested, and the ending leaves the door open for another chapter.

One thing season 2 certainly has going for it is its ambition. The series feels noticeably bigger this time around, with more varied settings, additional characters and some larger action sequences that give the story a different sense of scale. Not all of it lands, though, and some questionable special effects take away from the impact of certain locations and bigger moments. Thankfully, the cast and the underlying story are strong enough to make up for some of those shortcomings, keeping things engaging even when the visuals don’t quite deliver.

With the first season having covered the entirety of Stephen King’s original novel, the decision to take the story in a new direction gives the writers much more creative freedom. I think that mostly works in its favor, even if the results are a little uneven at times. There’s still plenty left to explore within this world, and the second season leaves enough doors open to make me curious about what comes next. There’s enough here to make another visit to the Institute worthwhile.

"The Institute" season 2 is streaming on MGM+, with new episodes arriving every Sunday.

Alix is a Senior Streaming Writer at Tom’s Guide, which basically means watching the best movies and TV shows and then writing about them. It’s a dream job for someone who’s been obsessed with storytelling since she first figured out how to work a remote.

Before joining Tom’s Guide, Alix honed her skills as a staff writer with outlets like Screen Rant and Bough Digital, where she discovered her love for the entertainment industry.

She heads to the cinema every week as a tradition, no matter what’s showing. For her, movies aren’t just entertainment — they’re a ritual, a comfort, and a constant source of inspiration. When she’s not at her desk or at the cinema, you’ll probably find her deep into a horror video game on her PC.

#3246. Guarding the Gates of Knowledge

AI can fake a plausible paper at the push of a button. Can detection tools and peer review keep up?

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.

Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.

Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.

“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland

As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”

Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.

Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.

“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”

If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.

Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

Harry Goldstein is Editor in Chief of IEEE Spectrum.

#3245. US charges three men over $129m scheme that faked CEOs’ voices with AI

Prosecutors in New York say the men posed as executives and lawyers on calls, then laundered the money through crypto.

The men are Jacob Soall, 41, Sharon Hazan, 54, and Guy Sheetrit, 42. Spanish police arrested Soall and Hazan in June and August, and UK police arrested Sheetrit in September. The US has asked for all three to be extradited.

The scheme ran from 2024 to 2026, according to the indictment. The men would call an employee while posing as the company’s chief executive, using AI to mimic the boss’s voice or image. They would ask for help with a secret deal.

The fake CEO then told the employee to contact a lawyer at a large international law firm. Another member of the group posed as that lawyer and gave the bank details for a large transfer.

The victims included a Missouri hospital system, which lost about $4.8m, and a UK fintech company, which lost about $11.6m. A Rhode Island bank, a California hospital system, a Massachusetts mutual fund, and a Florida pet food company were also hit.

The money went to accounts in countries including Spain, Greece, the UAE, Singapore, and China. It was then turned into cryptocurrency to hide where it came from, prosecutors said.

Soall mainly posed as UK lawyers and kept a handwritten script called Lawyer Call, according to the indictment. Hazan and Sheetrit are accused of laundering the money. Hazan was convicted of bank fraud conspiracy in the same court in 2008.

The three face charges including wire fraud, money laundering, and aggravated identity theft. The most serious counts carry up to 20 years in prison. The charges are allegations, and the men are presumed innocent.

The case is a larger version of a 2019 voice-cloning fraud, in which criminals faked a CEO’s voice to steal $243,000. Since then, AI impersonation scams have grown fast.

#3243. I tested Bose’s new entry-level soundbar — and while it has no Dolby Atmos, its dialogue clarity beats the Sonos Beam 2 for movies and Netflix shows

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen is the audio giant’s newest entry-level soundbar… but boy, oh boy, it doesn’t sound like one. The sound is surprisingly room-filling and powerful, and the bass boost mode enhances both streaming and 4K Blu-rays. Although it’s a teeny bit more expensive than I’d like, it sounds better than Sonos’ $480+ Beam 2.

More expansive than you’d think for a 3.0 channel

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Price: 3/5Sound quality: 4/5Design: 5/5Features: 4/5Overall score: 4/5Best for: Small spaces, small(ish) budgets

Soundbars are expensive. $800, $1,500, heck, I’ve even tested $3,500 models. That’s simply inaccessible for a lot of people. And not to mention size — some of the best soundbars are almost fifty inches long. I certainly don’t have that much space in my living room.

Thankfully, Bose has the answer for us small-budget, small-spaced folk. The Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen is just twenty-three inches long, making it ideal for cozy living rooms and smaller TVs. Nothing’s changed from the original — it’s still 23 inches long, 2 inches deep, and 4 inches high.

So what’s different? The 2nd Gen has a center tweeter for better dialogue and high-frequency sound separation. Sometimes I read these specs and resist the urge to roll my eyes, but in the TV Speaker 2nd Gen’s case, this new tweeter really does make a difference. I never struggled to hear dialogue, on-screen sound effects are surprisingly distinct, and the extra bass button is impactful.

There’s a lot I like about the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen.

Given its small stature, I wasn’t expecting room-filling sound from the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen. I was wrong.

As soon as I set it up with my TCL TV, I had floorboard-quaking sound. I watched three movies on 4K UHD Blu-rays — “Top Gun: Maverick”, “Project Hail Mary”, and “Obsession”, and watched basic stereo TV on Now TV (the U.K.’s HBO) and Netflix.

“Top Gun: Maverick” filled my testing room. I was super surprised by the expansiveness in the upper mids — the synth chords in the soundtrack came through with gusto. The rumbling of jet engines was impactful and didn’t overpower high-frequency sounds like clinking metal wheels and whirring equipment. While the whooshing ropes could have been a little louder, and I wanted a little more impact from the kick drum in the soundtrack, I was extremely happy with this performance — especially considering the soundbar’s 23 (L) x 2 (H) x 4 (D) size.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Dialogue was extremely clear, even in loud action sequences. When Maverick is flying at hypersonic, the rattling cockpit and screeching air resistance didn’t overpower the in-scene mumbled dialogue.

“Obsession” also sounded fantastic. The dialogue was perfectly clear, even in loud bar scenes underpinned with indistinct chatter and diegetic music. Every line filled the room. In quieter scenes, the crickets punctuated the fabric of the scene without overpowering the dialogue.

In “Project Hail Mary”, the soundtrack’s wind instrument sections were particularly overwhelming — in an intentional way. The whirring of the spaceship was audible even over the soundtrack, and I could really feel every layer of sound. Of course, this soundbar doesn’t have Dolby Atmos, but “behind” sounds, such as doors opening, sounded as if they were coming from behind me.

Stereo TV also sounded great. As not everyone has 4K Blu-rays — especially not if you need a small, cheap soundbar like this one — it’s only logical that I test it out on basic TV as well. “Supernatural” on Now TV has a great mixture of action sequences, broody dialogue, and soundtrack.

Even during action sequences, I could hear every word of dialogue. Of course, the overall quality was inferior compared to 4K Blu-rays, with everything a little more muffled.

I also watched “Gilmore Girls” on basic Netflix, which also has the 2.0 stereo audio track. As this is an older show, dialogue was a little softer, but this is also the case when I watch with my Denon Home 550 ($699).

The TV Speaker 2nd Gen has bass boost, which does what it says on the tin. I activated this for all my testing as it massively improved bass. Even with bass boost activated, the soundbar didn’t physically shake or peak, which can be an issue on cheaper models, such as the Ultimea Nova S50 ($129).

Thanks to its 23 x 2 x 4 inch stature, the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen would look at home in any cozy living room. At a push, it would look good with a 55-inch TV, but better with a 50-inch or 43-inch. Any bigger and the TV would dwarf the soundbar. If you have a 65-inch TV or bigger but you still want an affordable soundbar, I’d recommend the Samsung B550F ($225), which is 33 inches (and has a subwoofer).

The soundbar is also super light, so don’t worry about carrying the box up stairs or setting it up alone. I’m extremely weak, and I set it up by myself in seconds.

Although I was blown away by the big sound and impressed by the tiny footprint, the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen missed out on the perfect 5-star rating for a reason.

The Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen is $299 from Amazon U.S. and £299 from Amazon U.K. When I saw this price, I did a double take. As Bose’s entry-level soundbar, I think $299 is way too expensive. In the U.K., you can still buy 2021’s Bose Solo Soundbar II for £179, but it’s no longer sold in the U.S.

When the Sonos Ray — Sonos’ entry-level soundbar — is $219, it gets tricky to recommend the Bose. However, I tested the Sonos Beam 2 (a level up from the Ray) back-to-back, and the Bose sounded better. Do with that information what you will.

The original Bose TV Speaker is still available for $279 from Amazon — although I’m not sure how much longer — but, again, this isn’t cheap enough to undercut Sonos’ beginner soundbar.

Similarly, the Sony HT-S100F is one of the best cheap soundbars on the market, and it’s literally $119. Dialogue is clear, and while bass isn’t as powerful as the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen, you’re saving $180.

Don’t get me wrong, the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen really surprised me with its clarity and depth. However, $299 is still a lot of money for a first soundbar. I’m struggling to recommend it when Sonos and Sony’s entry-level options are so much cheaper.

If you can find the TV Speaker 2nd Gen on sale for around $200, it’s a no-brainer. But if you need a good soundbar for as little money as possible, I’d go for the Sony or Sonos.

While the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen has Bluetooth connectivity for streaming music from your phone, the Sonos Ray ($219) has AirPlay too. This means you can stream directly from the Spotify, Qobuz, Apple Music, or Tidal app. Of course, you can connect via Bluetooth, but this can be a little cumbersome. Fiddling around in your phone’s settings versus just clicking play from Qobuz is a no-brainer.

However — and there’s a big however coming — the Sonos Ray doesn’t have an HDMI connection. It connects to your TV using optical. Optical is generally considered to be inferior to HDMI for a few key reasons: optical cannot transfer Dolby Atmos or DTS:X, HDMI allows both audio and video, and if you have a DVD player with only an optical port, you’ll need to use an HDMI for your soundbar as your TV won’t have enough ports.

In short: just check what you need before buying any AV product.

Even so, both HDMI and optical are digital formats, so the audio quality should be around the same. On top of that, the TV Speaker 2nd Gen isn’t capable of Dolby Atmos anyway — it’s just 3.0 channels, while you need a minimum of 3.1.2 for Dolby Atmos — but it’s worth knowing.

I was lucky enough to test the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen and the Sonos Beam 2 back-to-back. Honestly? The Bose sounds better. Although the Sonos Beam 2 is more expansive, especially in the soundtrack and bass, its dialogue is a little harsher. I got fatigued faster while listening on the Sonos than the Bose.

High-frequency sounds are more abrasive on the Sonos. For long watching periods, I’d recommend the Bose. And you save $180! I’d also recommend investing an extra $70 in the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen over the Sonos Ray due to the latter’s lack of HDMI connection.

Of course, you can save a similar amount over the Bose with the Sony HT-S100F ($119), but the Bose has better bass depth. There’s also the Samsung B550F ($225), although I’ve not personally tested this model, so I can’t definitively tell you it’s better or worse.

Yes, if you value affordability and you have a TV 55 inches or smaller — 100% yes. I was genuinely surprised by the room-filling, powerful sound and the deftly controlled bass. The bass boost mode works really well, enhancing blockbuster movies from good to fantastic.

Sure, I wish there were AirPlay, but this is an entry-level soundbar, so we can’t be asking for the world. Despite the 2nd Gen only just coming out, maybe Bose can add AirPlay onto the 3rd Gen model. Just a thought… (coughBosecough).

Although it’s a little pricier than the Sonos and Sony competition, I wholeheartedly recommend the Bose TV Speaker 2nd Gen. I would happily switch out my Denon Home 550 ($699) for the Bose — and that’s saying something.
